items.title: Recap: Anthropic IPO, tech rout, Nvidia, and outage aftermath
items.summary:
Happy almost-Thanksgiving, after what frankly has been a helluva few weeks in tech. 

Personally, I’ve found the last couple news cycles to be surreal, strange, and consequential. As we’re barreling towards the holiday (and the very end of 2026), I reckoned it might be useful to distill down a few key thoughts about what the news of recent weeks might mean moving forward. 

Anthropic out, tech rout… Anthropic last week went public in a day-one 17% stock pop that mutated pretty quickly into a widespread tech rout. The Claude maker, still valued over $1 trillion even after its stock dropped 8% on Friday , instantaneously became an AI bellwether—and the broader market news was simply bad. The Nasdaq finished the week down 2.66% year-to-date, and both the Dow and the S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Expect volatility through the end of the year. 

I don’t know if the AI bubble will “officially” pop before Dec. 31, but we may well remember this moment as the instability before everything changed. Most of Anthropic’s employees may be paper millionaires, but it’s a rough road ahead. 

Life after Jensen has commenced… After Jensen Huang’s shocking ouster, Nvidia reported earnings last week, revealing beats across the board. This muted some of the deepest fears about Nvidia’s near-term future, but that earnings win doesn’t change much, as questions about the company’s future abound: Can Nvidia be relied upon to carry on as AI’s central bank, for both startups and data center financing deals? What will happen to neoclouds like CoreWeave and Lambda Labs without Huang as…
items.t: Recap: Anthropic IPO, tech rout, Nvidia, and outage aftermath

items.title: Scott Bessent has changed his tune on Nvidia leadership as President Trump says chipmaker should ‘rehire’ Huang
items.summary:
The Trump administration has officially backed Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia—a little over a week after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the AI giant needed a “dramatic shake-up” of leadership. 

Huang and Nvidia, the company he founded in 1993, are currently subject to intense scrutiny after it emerged that Huang had conducted an extramarital affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy. The company and its leadership are now facing questions from Congress and U.S. law enforcement about their compliance with export controls on specialized chips to China.

But olive branches are now being extended to Huang, not only from within the AI community but now also at the highest level of government.

President Trump wrote on Truth Social this morning: “I hope the board of Nvidia rehires Jensen Huang. It would be the best thing for the company, and also, for the U.S.A.” 

The president has been lenient on Huang, despite Congressional concerns that Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese asset was a national security risk. Nvidia has said it does not believe U.S. or company secrets have been compromised. Despite that, Trump said he is a “brilliant person” who made some “bad decisions.”

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also took a softer approach on Huang in an interview over the weekend. Bessent had previously said Nvidia directors needed to look externally for a candidate to lead the company, but sought to recast that stance: “Jensen is on the outside now,” he told CBS yesterday.

“I said they should go to the outside, but he’s on the outside now,” Bessent added.…
items.t: Scott Bessent has changed his tune on Nvidia leadership as President Trump says chipmaker should ‘rehire’ Huang

items.title: People are injecting ‘research use only’ peptides from random websites. I run a pharmacy and see the gray market up close
items.summary:
Americans are using peptides regardless of FDA approval. They’re ordering them online, sharing experiences on social media, and listening to influencer advice instead of a physician’s. In some cases, people are injecting “research use only” labeled substances into their bodies without any meaningful assurance of what the product is or where it came from.

This is the reality we’re dealing with, and pretending otherwise isn’t making anyone safer.

Ana Santos Rutschman, a legal professor at Villanova University recently published an opinion piece in Fortune that suggested the federal government’s decision to expand access to six peptides through compounding pharmacies would provide virtually no regulatory protection for customers. As a pharmacist, I agree these substances deserve scrutiny. Their safety and effectiveness have not been established, and customers should understand there is more to the conversation besides each peptide’s individual promotion. But the article’s suggestion that compounding pharmacies operate with little to “no regulation” is hyperbole. More importantly, this claim overlooks the role that responsible, vetted pharmacies can play in making an already-existing market safer.

My pharmacy, Cody Drug, has a financial interest in this conversation. We began dispensing peptides covered by the new federal policy after it was announced. But being a part of the peptide conversation from a pharmaceutical perspective means that no shortcuts should be taken when it comes to sterile compounding operations, sourcing ingredients, and dispensing finished medication.…
items.t: People are injecting ‘research use only’ peptides from random websites. I run a pharmacy and see the gray market up close

items.title: Your brand is famous. That’s not why people buy it
items.summary:
Coca-Cola’s global CMO Manolo Arroyo said something at the ANA Masters of Marketing last month that many marketers only think. “I do not believe any more in love,” he told the room. Love, he explained, “follows the behavior.” Coca-Cola now steers by weekly penetration.

He’s right. Plenty of people adore brands they never buy.

But context matters. Coca-Cola has spent more than a century building one of the most differentiated brands on earth. For Coke, the reason to choose is already built in. Most brands don’t start there, and I worry about the lesson their boardrooms may take. Budgets for 2027 are being locked this month, and earnings calls are rewarding anything that moves the quarter. The easy conclusion is that if love doesn’t matter, reach is the whole job.

That conclusion is wrong, and it is getting expensive. Across the global brands I work with, companies are spending more to be seen and less to be chosen. They buy awareness and reach because those are easy to measure and easy to defend to a CFO. What goes unfunded is a clear reason to pick their brand over the next one, the thing that turns attention into growth and growth into margin. That is “difference,” and most of the market is looking at it wrong.

It is also getting scarcer. Kantar’s data shows perceived difference across brands has fallen almost 20% over the past decade. The likely culprit is marketing tuned for algorithms, and now AI, that makes brands look and sound alike. Call it a differentiation crisis. It should alarm every boardroom, because brands that look the same end up competing on price.…
items.t: Your brand is famous. That’s not why people buy it

items.title: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit
items.summary:
Elon Musk’s foundation gave away nearly $400 million in 2025, and more than three-quarters of it went to another nonprofit he founded, according to the Musk Foundation’s latest tax filing , first reported by Bloomberg.

That total is down from the record $474 million the foundation gave in 2024. Over the same year, its assets grew by more than $1 billion, to about $16 billion, helped by a $64 million gift of Tesla shares. That makes it one of the world’s largest private foundations.

The gap between what the foundation holds and what it gives matters because private foundations must generally pay out about 5% of their investment assets each year or face IRS excise taxes . The Musk Foundation has fallen short of that minimum before, Forbes reported after reviewing its 2024 filing . Foundations can make up a shortfall the following year, so one year’s giving doesn’t settle whether the rule was met.

The foundation runs with almost no staff. Its tax return lists three directors: Musk, his family-office head Jared Birchall, and Matilda Simon. Musk, who is also listed as president, reported working for the foundation about an hour a week, Bloomberg reported.

Where the money went 

More than $310 million went to The Foundation, a nonprofit Musk set up to run a STEM-focused primary and secondary school in Bastrop, Texas, outside Austin, with plans to eventually add a university .

Another $20 million went to a donor-advised fund at Fidelity Charitable over which Musk has advisory control. Donors to these funds can take a tax deduction when they contribute and later recommend…
items.t: Elon Musk spends about an hour a week on his $16 billion foundation. Most of its 2025 giving went to another Musk nonprofit

Good morning . U.S. markets are in correction territory, with the S&P 500 down more than 11% since its October highs, and the Nasdaq Composite down about 18%. Take your pick of culprits: AI spending, the Nvidia turmoil, trade tensions, the midterm fallout, sticky inflation. 

While S&P 500 futures suggest there could be a bounce today, stocks could be volatile for some time. Here’s what to watch:

The AI ecosystem. Nvidia shares kept sliding, but the pain also spread to stocks like Caterpillar , which now trades like an AI infrastructure stock because so much of its growth comes from data centers. The company’s stock fell 5% Friday and is down about 28% over the past month. Data center opposition was a winning issue in several midterm races, meaning future deals could face more friction. For those who supply cooling equipment, power generation and other data center infrastructure, the question is which companies already have financing and approval. Nvidia’s deals with specialized AI cloud providers, or neoclouds, are contingent on those customers securing financing. And Nvidia itself is backing deals, though the details are often fuzzy, making it hard to predict how Nvidia’s lower valuation ripples through customers whose deals depend on its backing.

The bond market. When investors flee stocks, they often shift…

items.title: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said
items.summary:
Morgan Freeman has arguably the most recognizable voice in Hollywood—and that’s made him a frequent target for AI copycats.

“You can create artists and make them say things they never said, which has happened to me,” Freeman told Fortune . 

Freeman isn’t against the technology itself. He and longtime producing partner Lori McCreary have spent decades putting new tools to work in filmmaking through their movie production company, Revelations Entertainment. The issue, he said, is privacy.

“What we should be doing with technology is what we actually are dreaming of doing,” he said. “But we have to somehow protect privacy, and that’s the first thing that loses its grip.”

McCreary, who cofounded Revelations Entertainment with Freeman in 1996, said AI is different from the tools that came before it. About two and a half years ago, she came across a clip online she didn’t remember Freeman filming, so she called to ask him about it. 

“He was like, ‘I don’t remember.’ And that was the first time when I thought, ‘Okay, we’ve got to get ahead of this,’” McCreary told Fortune .

Freeman has pushed back about AI copies of his voice, too. Last November, Freeman told The Guardian his lawyers had been “very, very busy” and had found “quite a few” instances of his voice being replicated without his consent. And in June 2024, he also thanked fans on X for calling out unauthorized AI imitations of his voice. 

McCreary said they now get calls every day about people selling products online using Freeman’s voice, which he has no connection to. AI can reproduce his voice and his…
items.t: Morgan Freeman says AI should do ‘what we actually are dreaming of doing’—but deepfakes have also made him say things he never said

items.title: After the Palisades fire, a founder built AI to help survivors with paperwork. Now he needs a state to buy it
items.summary:
When the Palisades fire tore through his Los Angeles neighborhood in January 2025, Jonathon Nostrant’s house was damaged but still standing. Many of his neighbors’ homes were destroyed.

The fire was only the first ordeal. Next, Nostrant found a tangle of federal, state, and local assistance programs, each with its own forms, eligibility rules, and deadlines. Survivors with insurance must also report their payouts to every agency they apply to, because FEMA cannot pay for losses an insurer already covers.

Insurance was already a sore subject in the Palisades. A year before the fire, State Farm dropped roughly 1,600 policies in the neighborhood, Fortune reported as the fire burned .

“Our insurance was fighting with us,” Nostrant said in an interview, describing his own claim.

That experience led to AidFinder, a Miami-based startup Nostrant co-founded that uses AI to match disaster survivors with programs they may qualify for, explain eligibility rules, and prepare applications. Survivors review everything before submission. The intended customers, though, are states, which would offer the platform to residents under their own banner.

For now, it is a pitch. AidFinder hasn’t signed its first state customer, and survivors have yet to use the platform, Refresh Miami reported on Nov. 17 . Nostrant told the outlet the company is in talks with 30 states, including Florida, and that Craig Fugate, who ran FEMA under President Barack Obama, has accepted a seat on its board.

A voice-tech veteran takes on paperwork 

Nostrant has spent much of his career teaching machines to…
items.t: After the Palisades fire, a founder built AI to help survivors with paperwork. Now he needs a state to buy it

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary:
Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment

Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be.

All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict. But well within living memory a combination of the power of trade unions and the collective social conscience built into the postwar consensus resulted in an economy and labour market that now seem almost inconceivable. For sure they were scattered with restrictive practices and base prejudice: fathers securing jobs for their sons, people from minorities being excluded from work not just by people in management but by their fellow workers, and a great deal of…

items.title: I hated life as a Neet. But now I’ve found a job, life is just as precarious | Emilija Morrison
items.summary:
The government’s plans to help young people not in education, work or training are welcome – I dearly hope they offer long-term security

  • Emilija Morrison is a University of Glasgow graduate and holds a Gold Standard NCTJ Diploma in journalism

What child dreams of being unemployed when they grow up? You can probably remember the days, aged 10, when you were asked to present to the class what you wanted to be. Imagine hearing this: “I want to be unemployed. After I graduate from university, I want to go to the jobcentre in my home town and collect my benefits every month.”

Yet that is the reality for many young people today – childhood dreams to become a teacher, a doctor, an engineer or whatever other profession thwarted not by the limits of their abilities, but the reality of the economy.

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage

items.title: iPhone designer Tony Fadell’s next big thing: Bringing AI to fashion in hopes of saving H&M $100 million a year
items.summary:
The fashion business thrives on the conceit that it is modern, on-trend, and all about what’s happening right now . But behind the scenes—in the textile mills and garment factories that supply major brands—is an industry that runs much as it did in the 1970s. Its supply chains are splintered, chaotic, and based in warehouses that are so old-fashioned they may not even be on the internet, according to Max Easton, CEO of Smartex.AI.

Most of the work is done by hand. Checking the quality of the fabric, for instance, will be performed by a worker holding a handful of color swatches, watching a roll of cloth go by all day.

“They’re looking for simple physical defects like holes, needles, the wrong yarn, something that would be noticeable in a garment, right?” Easton said to Fortune at Web Summit in Lisbon this year. For most brands, there is no such thing as a “white” T-shirt. It needs to be exactly the right shade of white—which might be a brilliant white or a creamier off-white.

But because the work is inspected by humans, fashion brands can never be quite sure that the quality of the fabric they’re buying is going to be consistent, or even match what they ordered.

“If you go to any kind of [fashion] supply chain, whether it’s fabric production or garment production, most people are just kind of amazed by how chaotic it is,” Easton said.

The chaos ends now, Smartex hopes. 

The company has been working with Tony Fadell, the legendary codesigner of the iPod, iPhone, and Nest doorbell, to launch a physical AI product that can perform fabric quality checks continuously, at…
